name: lips60-copy
brief:
The article's concrete detail: Shopify: Debezium CDC across 100+ MySQL shards lands in Kafka under 10s p99.

Kai Waehner splits truth for AI agents across three systems: the transactional database, Apache Kafka, and the lakehouse. The database is the teller moving the money, Kafka the ticker announcing every move, the lakehouse the archive of old statements. Debezium CDC keeps the ticker fed, and the agent reads state from a serving table while sending requests back through the log.

My one condition: the ticker only helps if you can see how far behind it runs. Kafka earns its place for agents when CDC lag, replay and command flow are observable end to end — otherwise the serving table is a departure board nobody updates, and the agent trusts a flight that already left.

On writes, the rule is short: the agent asks, the system of record decides, in one transaction. Shopify proves the pattern at scale, pushing changes from a 100-plus shard MySQL monolith into Kafka in under ten seconds at the 99th percentile.

I'd be glad to hear how other teams surface lag to their agent layer, since my thresholds only got honest after stale data fooled me.

Source here: https://www.kai-waehner.de/blog/2026/11/13/kafka-and-database-truth-for-ai-agents/

# Scenes and the storyboard

Motion rules (apply to every scene):
# Motion rules

Craft rules for an authored composition. They apply to every scene; they are not a
checklist to report back.

- **Nothing fully stops.** A still final frame is the biggest tell an authored clip
  has. End on an ambient idle — a slow breathe, drift or sheen — rather than a hold.
- **Keep one continuous camera move underneath the scene** and never let it decay to a
  stop; a move that eases to zero reads as frozen.
- **Stagger entrances at offsets shorter than the animations they offset**, so an
  arrival reads as one overlapping wave instead of a queue.
- **Compound a property only when it tells one story** — position and scale moving one
  object. Do not stack unrelated changes on an element for their own sake.
- **Overshoot belongs on transforms, never on a number.** A counter settles on its
  value; a scale pop may pass it. Keep overshoot rare and playful, not the default.
- **Build depth from planes with a real foreground occlusion** — something in front of
  something else — not from size alone.
- **Match the pacing to the content.** A calm idea moves slowly; a punchy one snaps.
  Read the brief for the tone.
- **Seed imperfection where a handmade feel is wanted**, with an index-derived offset —
  never a clock and never unseeded randomness.

## A still is read at rest

When the brief asks for a still, its final state is the artifact: compose it complete and let
nothing animate. An article page carries one moving visual, its lead image; every section
figure beside it is still, and its labels are read at the width it is rendered at.

## Prove it

`check` verifies motion only when the composition ships a sidecar, so ship one:
`index.motion.json` beside the composition, matching its basename. Assert the intent —
`appearsBy` that each subject is on screen when its scene needs it, `staysInFrame` that
it stays there, `keepsMoving` that no shot freezes — then run `check` once after lint is
clean and fix every finding before you report. With no sidecar the motion audit does not
run, and `check` passes a clip whose subjects never reach the screen.

`staysInFrame` reads a box from the moment the element is half-opaque, so an entrance
that travels in from off-canvas must still be under that opacity while it is outside the
canvas.

Never put `data-layout-allow-overflow` on an element that clips its children
(`overflow: hidden`): the hatch silences the clipping findings for everything inside it,
which is how content that never renders passes the gate. Mark the travelling element, or
put the hatch on a wrapper that does not clip.

name: connector-head
brief:
The design decision Kai Waehner lays out is how to give an AI agent both the present and the recent past: the transactional database as the system of record, Apache Kafka as the event log in and out, and the lakehouse for history. The database decides the refund in one transaction, Kafka carries each committed change as an ordered, replayable event, and the serving table built from the topic answers the agent's key lookups without touching the source.

Where I would hold the line is on visibility. Kafka earns its place for agents only when CDC lag, replay and the command flow are observable end to end, and an unmeasured serving table is just another stale copy wearing a real-time label. The failure is quiet: every read succeeds, the audit trail looks clean, and the agent has already acted on a balance that changed minutes ago.

The write side keeps a rule worth stealing. The agent publishes requests such as refund requested; only the system of record publishes facts such as refund issued, inside its own transaction, so no dual write can split the two systems. Shopify's CDC platform shows the whole pattern holding under load, moving changes from a 100-plus shard MySQL monolith into Kafka in under ten seconds at the 99th percentile.

I'd be glad to hear how other teams expose lag and freshness to their agent layer, since my own thresholds only earned trust after stale data slipped past them once.

Source here: https://www.kai-waehner.de/blog/2026/11/13/kafka-and-database-truth-for-ai-agents/

name: sketch-clean
brief:
A homelab data pipeline in four moves. dlt reads a supplier's invoice feed and lands it in bronze as raw JSON, one row per invoice, line items still nested. dbt parses that JSON into silver invoice tables, expands each invoice into its line items, and tests the totals against the header. A gold model rolls the line items up per month and per supplier, and Superset reads only gold. Trino sits underneath all of it and grants each user its own catalogue scope, so the dashboard user never sees bronze.

- `retro`: draw it as a 16-bit console screen - chunky pixel art on a coarse grid, a small palette, hard-edged HUD frames and bitmap lettering, each subject snapping in on its own beat.
- `launch`: announce a thing we ship - one brand lockup, one status badge, a headline with its supporting line, the feature set as a few short chips, a window of the product's own interface with the working part accented, and one call to action.
- `tiles`: fill the frame edge to edge with a named generative tiling - a Truchet tiling (quarter-arc tiles), a zellige interlace, a labyrinth - recognisable as the thing it is named and reading as one continuous drawing rather than repeated separate motifs, orientation and tone set by a seeded walk, under a technical HUD frame that names the pattern and its seed, sits outside the field and keeps the frame's outer edge clear.
- `sketch`: draw it as a sketched diagram - labelled boxes, arrows and connectors on a wobbly ink stroke whose wobble is a seeded, index-derived offset rather than a random one, the strokes drawing themselves on in reading order and settling into a drawing that stays legible, with no shading, gradient or photographic fill and one slow camera drift to the end.

How scenes work:
# Scenes and the storyboard

A scene is one beat of the composition: one idea, one arrangement, held long enough to
read. Scenes play in the order the storyboard names.

- Plan the storyboard before authoring: the form, the scenes and the order they play in.
- One idea per scene. Do not split one idea across two scenes, and do not put two ideas in
  one scene.
- A declared count names content scenes. The opening title scene, when the brief asks for
  one, is additional to them and sits before them.
- A scene has no fixed length; give each the time its idea needs to read, and keep the
  composition's total to the declared duration.

## Copy on screen

A clip is watched, not read: the scene leaves before anyone finishes a sentence, so the
words must land in the time it has.

- One line per scene, six words at most, plus one figure when the idea is a number.
- Put the outcome on screen, not the explanation: "3x faster", "one pipeline", "zero
  retries". The sentence behind it belongs in the post text.
- Type is the message. Size the line to be read at phone width in the first second, and
  give the rest of the frame to the subject and its motion.
- One short label names a thing that moves; never caption it.
- These govern what plays: a video, a GIF and a deck's rendered video. A slide the reader
  clicks through may carry its supporting points, and an SVG on a page may carry a label.
Style: use the brand's dark scheme; do not introduce a colour or typeface the brand block below does not define.
Use a 1280x720 (16:9) viewBox.
Animate with CSS @keyframes inside a <style> element, or with SMIL; no external stylesheet, no script, no network. Reveal a few elements in sequence, each held long enough to read.
Reference the brand typefaces by name with a system fallback, and keep the file well-formed XML with every animated element ending visible.
Motion rules (apply to every scene):
# Motion rules

Craft rules for an authored composition. They apply to every scene; they are not a
checklist to report back.

- **Nothing fully stops.** A still final frame is the biggest tell an authored clip
  has. End on an ambient idle — a slow breathe, drift or sheen — rather than a hold.
- **Keep one continuous camera move underneath the scene** and never let it decay to a
  stop; a move that eases to zero reads as frozen.
- **Stagger entrances at offsets shorter than the animations they offset**, so an
  arrival reads as one overlapping wave instead of a queue.
- **Compound a property only when it tells one story** — position and scale moving one
  object. Do not stack unrelated changes on an element for their own sake.
- **Overshoot belongs on transforms, never on a number.** A counter settles on its
  value; a scale pop may pass it. Keep overshoot rare and playful, not the default.
- **Build depth from planes with a real foreground occlusion** — something in front of
  something else — not from size alone.
- **Match the pacing to the content.** A calm idea moves slowly; a punchy one snaps.
  Read the brief for the tone.
- **Seed imperfection where a handmade feel is wanted**, with an index-derived offset —
  never a clock and never unseeded randomness.

## Prove it

`check` verifies motion only when the composition ships a sidecar, so ship one:
`index.motion.json` beside the composition, matching its basename. Assert the intent —
`appearsBy` that each subject is on screen when its scene needs it, `staysInFrame` that
it stays there, `keepsMoving` that no shot freezes — then run `check` once after lint is
clean and fix every finding before you report. With no sidecar the motion audit does not
run, and `check` passes a clip whose subjects never reach the screen.

`staysInFrame` reads a box from the moment the element is half-opaque, so an entrance
that travels in from off-canvas must still be under that opacity while it is outside the
canvas.

Never put `data-layout-allow-overflow` on an element that clips its children
(`overflow: hidden`): the hatch silences the clipping findings for everything inside it,
which is how content that never renders passes the gate. Mark the travelling element, or
put the hatch on a wrapper that does not clip.
